Introduction: Shifting our Focus to Treatment

Welcome back, everyone! I was looking through the survey responses you submitted during our first lecture, and I noticed a distinct trend: a vast majority of you are incredibly curious about the treatment side of nanomedicine. We’ve spent the last few weeks exploring how we diagnose diseases and how we fabricate nanoscale materials. Now, it is time to bring those concepts together and look at how we actually treat diseases.

When we talk about nanomedicine, the single biggest market and area of research is cancer treatment. So, today, we are going to focus our lens entirely on cancer. Our goals are straightforward: we need to understand the basic terminology, identify the different types of cancer, and explore the underlying “hallmarks” that make a cancer cell behave the way it does. Why does this matter for a nanoscience class? Because once we understand these hallmarks, we can exploit them to design targeted nanomedicines that attack the cancer while leaving healthy tissue alone.

Before we get into the nanoscale engineering, let’s start with a fundamental question. Think about your own life, the news, or stories you’ve heard. What actually is cancer?

At its core, cancer is the uncontrolled growth of cells. It is a disease where abnormal cells divide without their usual regulatory checkpoints, growing uncontrollably and eventually destroying surrounding healthy body tissue. It creates a new mass of tissue—often referred to as a tumor or a neoplasm—that does not belong to our original body plan.

The Language of Cancer: Key Terminologies

To navigate the world of nanomedicine, we need to speak the language of the medical field. Let’s break down a few critical terms you will encounter constantly in this space.

  • Oncology: The prefix onco- means mass, bulk, or tumor, and -logy means the study of. Therefore, oncology is the branch of medicine dealing with the prevention, diagnosis, and treatment of cancer.

  • Metastasis: This is a word you will hear often in nanomedicine research. Metastatic cancer is cancer that has spread from its original, primary site to other parts of the body. It is incredibly serious and very difficult to remove surgically. A major goal of nanomedicine is to design particles that can circulate in the bloodstream to hunt down and kill these metastatic cells wherever they hide.

  • Apoptosis: This is actually a neutral, healthy word! It means programmed cell death. Normal cells have a built-in self-destruct sequence when they become too old or damaged. Cancer cells, however, figure out how to turn this program off.

  • Angiogenesis: As we mentioned in previous lectures, tumors are hungry. They need a massive supply of glucose and oxygen to sustain their rapid growth. Angiogenesis is the physiological process where tumors signal the body to build new blood vessels from pre-existing ones, essentially building their own private supply highways to steal nutrients from the rest of the body.

Types and Causes of Cancer

Cancer is not just one disease; it is a collection of related diseases that we categorize based on where they originate in the body.

We generally divide them into a few broad categories:

  1. Carcinoma: These start in the skin or the tissues that line other organs (like the lungs, breasts, or stomach).

  2. Sarcoma: These are cancers of connective tissues, such as bones, muscles, cartilage, and blood vessels.

  3. Leukemia: This is a cancer of the bone marrow, which is responsible for creating our blood cells. You will typically find this manifesting in the bloodstream.

  4. Lymphoma: This is related to the immune system and the lymph nodes. Because the lymphatic system is a network that spreads throughout the body, lymphomas are notoriously difficult to isolate and treat.

Worldwide, the six most common cancers are lung, colon, breast, prostate, stomach, and liver cancer. Interestingly, the prevalence varies by region and culture. For example, in some Asian regions where drinking very hot water or tea is common, we see a higher rate of stomach and esophageal cancers.

This brings us to our next question: What actually causes these cells to go rogue?

Cancer is generally triggered by environmental factors that damage our cells. We can group these into three agents:

  • Physical agents: This includes UV radiation from the sun, X-rays, and other forms of ionizing radiation.

  • Chemical agents: Tobacco smoke is a massive one. But as scientists and engineers, we also need to be aware of the organic solvents and chemicals we use in the lab. Always wear your PPE and avoid direct contact with hazardous chemicals!

  • Biological agents: Certain viruses and bacteria can cause cancer. A prime example is HPV (Human Papillomavirus), which is a known cause of cervical and other cancers.

The Hallmarks of Cancer

To fight cancer, we have to understand its fundamental characteristics, which researchers call the “hallmarks of cancer.” Today, we are going to look closely at two of them: genetic mutations and deregulating cellular metabolism.

Hallmark 1: Genetic Mutations

To understand genetic mutations, we need to zoom all the way down to the nanoscale—to the DNA itself. Humans have 23 pairs of chromosomes (46 in total), which contain roughly 20,000 to 23,000 genes.

DNA is built from four nucleobases: Cytosine (C), Guanine (G), Adenine (A), and Thymine (T). When DNA is transcribed into RNA, the structure is similar but single-stranded, and Thymine is replaced by Uracil (U).

How does this information become a living, breathing human? We follow the Central Dogma of biology.

DNA is transcribed into mRNA, which is then translated into proteins. Proteins are the final products that perform specific functions in our bodies. However, every time a cell divides, it has to duplicate its entire DNA. During this replication, or when exposed to external damage, errors can occur.

If UV light hits a DNA strand, it can physically modify the base pairs. We classify these mutations into two types:

  1. Somatic mutations: These happen in your regular body cells (everything except eggs and sperm). If a skin cell mutates from UV exposure, it passes that mutation to its daughter cells when it divides. You cannot pass this to your children.

  2. Germline mutations: These occur in the germ cells (eggs or sperm) and are inherited by offspring. For example, inheriting a mutated BRCA1/2 gene increases the risk of breast cancer, and a mutated CDH1 gene increases the risk of stomach cancer.

Notice my phrasing: inheriting the gene puts you at an increased risk. The gene itself doesn’t instantly cause cancer. Cancer is caused by an accumulation of detrimental variations over time.

To understand how these mutations lead to uncontrolled growth, think of a cell like a car.

Every cell has two types of genes controlling its division:

  • Oncogenes: These are the gas pedal. When activated, they tell the cell to divide.

  • Tumor Suppressor Genes: These are the brakes. When activated, they tell the cell to stop dividing or to undergo apoptosis.

In a normal cell, the gas is lightly pressed, and the brakes work perfectly. In a cancer cell, a mutation jams the gas pedal all the way down (over-expressed oncogenes) and completely cuts the brake lines (lost or mutated tumor suppressor genes).

Hallmark 2: Deregulating Cellular Metabolism

Let’s tie this back to our diagnosis lectures. Remember when we talked about Positron Emission Tomography (PET) scans? We used a radioactive tracer called FDG (Fluorine-18 fluorodeoxyglucose). Why did we use a modified sugar molecule to find cancer?

We use glucose because of the second hallmark: deregulated cellular metabolism. Cancer cells are incredibly greedy for energy.

Normally, when plenty of oxygen is available, our cells use glucose to produce a massive amount of energy (ATP) and carbon dioxide. If you are sprinting and run out of oxygen, your muscles switch to an anaerobic process that produces less energy and a byproduct called lactate (lactic acid)—which is why your muscles burn during a heavy workout.

Cancer cells, however, do something very strange. Even when they have plenty of oxygen, they choose to process glucose into lactate. This phenomenon is called the Warburg Effect. Because this process is inefficient at making energy, the cancer cell has to consume vast amounts of glucose to survive—which is exactly why they light up on a PET scan!

Why this matters for nanomedicine: Because the tumor is constantly pumping out lactic acid, the microenvironment immediately surrounding a tumor is highly acidic (low pH). As engineers, we can design “smart” nanoparticles that remain perfectly stable in the neutral pH of the bloodstream but dissolve and release their toxic drug payload the moment they enter the acidic environment of the tumor!

Treating Cancer with Nanotechnology

Historically, we have relied on a few blunt instruments to treat cancer: surgery (cutting it out), radiotherapy (burning it with radiation), and chemotherapy (poisoning the whole body and hoping the cancer dies before the patient does).

Today, we are moving toward personalized therapy. By understanding the specific mutations and proteins present on a patient’s unique cancer cells, we can design nanoparticles that actively seek out those specific cells.

We achieve this through active tumor targeting. We decorate the outside of our nanoparticles with “ligands”—molecules that act like a key looking for a specific lock (receptor) on the cancer cell’s surface.

  • Antibodies: Large proteins that bind with high specificity to antigens on the cancer cell.

  • Non-Antibodies: Smaller molecules like vitamins (folate), carbohydrates (galactosamine), or peptides (RGD) that tumors naturally crave and have receptors for.

  • Aptamers: These are fascinating nanoscale tools. They are short, single strands of DNA or RNA that fold into complex 3D shapes. Because of their unique shape, they can trap and bind to specific target molecules just like an antibody, but they are entirely synthetic and highly stable.

Once we have our targeting ligand, how do we actually deliver the drug?

We have two main strategies for loading the drug onto our nanocarriers:

  1. Drug Conjugation: The drug molecules are chemically attached to the outside surface of the nanoparticle.

  2. Drug Encapsulation (Entrapment): The drug is stuffed inside the hollow core of the nanoparticle. This is generally the preferred method because it protects the drug from degrading in the bloodstream and usually allows for a much higher loading efficiency (we can pack more drug into a single particle).

We can build these carriers out of many different materials depending on the job. We can use carbon nanotubes, biodegradable polymers, or liposomes (spheres made of lipids, similar to our own cell membranes). By combining a high-capacity nanocarrier, a smart pH-responsive release mechanism, and a highly specific targeting ligand, we can deliver devastating payloads directly to the cancer cells while leaving the rest of the body completely unharmed.
